title: NAT and PAT: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Your whole office shares one public address, yet everyone browses the web. So how does a reply find the right person? Meet the mail room clerk.

scenes.heading: The mail room clerk
scenes.narration: A building with a thousand residents has one street address. The clerk logs each outgoing package with the resident's flat number and a package number. Then the clerk relabels it with the building's address and a new number. When the reply comes back, the clerk checks the log and sends it to the right flat. That log is the N A T table.

items.story: Reply goes to the right flat

scenes.heading: Three types of NAT
scenes.narration: There are three flavours of N A T. Static is a permanent one to one swap. Dynamic borrows an address from a pool, one to one. And P A T, also called overload, shares one address between many hosts, using port numbers.

steps.title: Dynamic
steps.sub: One to one, from a pool

scenes.heading: PAT in a few lines
scenes.narration: Here's the P A T setup. Mark which interface faces inside. And which faces outside. Match your private hosts with an access list. Then overload the outside interface. Check it with show I P nat translations.

lines.t: ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/1 overload

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three slip-ups. P A T and dynamic N A T aren't the same thing. The access list matches your private addresses, not the public ones. And static N A T never times out.

items.wrong: PAT and dynamic NAT are the same
items.right: PAT shares one address using ports
It stays until you remove it

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. N A T swaps private addresses for public ones. P A T lets many hosts share one public address, using port numbers. And the N A T table is how replies find their way back. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva NAT lab.
